assessment.nobel_worthiness: IceCube turned a cubic kilometre of Antarctic ice into a neutrino telescope and opened a genuinely new observational window: a diffuse astrophysical neutrino flux, and evidence for neutrino emission from TXS 0506+056, NGC 1068 and the Galactic plane. This is the kind of instrument-driven discovery I value most; it took decades of patient detector development, calibration and control of atmospheric backgrounds.
assessment.attribution: Halzen is the scientific driver and long-time spokesperson/PI who conceived and carried the full-scale detector; Spiering is credited for the foundational Baikal and DUMAND-era work and for the neutrino-telescope concept in Europe. A two-person prize looks defensible, but the collaboration is large and the role of other founders (e.g. early AMANDA and Baikal leaders) is something I cannot fully verify from the supplied text.
assessment.maturity: The diffuse flux has been confirmed in several independent channels and by the ANTARES/Baikal-GVD and KM3NeT efforts in part. Source associations are at 3-4 sigma level and still being refined, but the discovery of the flux itself is solid and recognition would be timely.
uncertainties: Individual-source identifications are less than 5 sigma and their interpretation is still evolving.
Whether the decisive credit is limited to Halzen and Spiering, or should include others in the early AMANDA/Baikal/DUMAND programmes.
Relation to the 2002 prize for cosmic neutrinos (Davis, Koshiba) and how the committee views a second neutrino-astronomy award.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical lattice clocks, built on Katori's magic-wavelength idea, reached fractional uncertainties near 1e-18 and now outperform caesium by orders of magnitude. They are a precision-measurement tool with clear lasting impact for tests of fundamental physics, relativistic geodesy and the planned redefinition of the second.
assessment.attribution: Katori proposed and first demonstrated the magic-wavelength lattice clock concept, a decisive originating contribution. Ye brought the clock to record accuracy and stability and did much to develop it into a flagship instrument. A two-person configuration is clean and fair, though Hall and Hansch (2005) already recognised the frequency comb side and Ye's role overlaps with other clock groups.
assessment.maturity: Many independent groups at NIST, JILA, PTB, RIKEN, SYRTE and elsewhere confirm the performance and compare clocks. The technique is stable and mature, and recognition would be timely.
uncertainties: Possible overlap with the 2012 (Wineland, ion-trap clock work) and 2005 prizes, and competition from trapped-ion optical clocks and the thorium nuclear clock.
Whether Ye's contribution is better described as the decisive realisation or as one of several leading groups; I rely on colleagues in atomic physics for this.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Localising gamma-ray bursts to arcminutes with BeppoSAX, followed by X-ray, optical and radio afterglows, settled the long-standing question of their distance and showed they are cosmological, the most energetic explosions since the Big Bang. This was decided by an instrument: a wide-field camera plus rapid-pointing narrow-field telescopes. It is close to my own area and I think it is highly worthy.
assessment.attribution: Costa (Wide Field Cameras and the first X-ray afterglow in 1997) and Frontera (Gamma-Ray Burst Monitor and BeppoSAX GRB programme) were the decisive instrument and discovery leaders. Kulkarni led the radio and optical identification, redshift and energetics work. Optical afterglow discoverers (van Paradijs, Groot) and Djorgovski and Metzger on the redshift side complicate the allocation, and one of the key people has died, which narrows the field.
assessment.maturity: Afterglows and cosmological origin have been confirmed by thousands of events, Swift and Fermi. The interpretation is stable and the discovery is nearly three decades old, so it is not premature.
uncertainties: Fair allocation among BeppoSAX leaders and the ground-based afterglow teams is contentious.
Some principal discoverers may no longer be eligible.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Theory by Bistritzer and MacDonald predicted flat bands at the magic angle, and Jarillo-Herrero's group then found correlated insulators and superconductivity in twisted bilayer graphene. This created the field of moire quantum materials with a tunable platform and a large, lasting experimental and theoretical impact.
assessment.attribution: A clean theory-plus-experiment story: Bistritzer-MacDonald for the flat-band prediction and Jarillo-Herrero for the experimental discovery. Cory Dean, Philip Kim and Dean's hBN-moire work, and Santos and Lopes dos Santos, complicate the credit, so the three names given may not be the complete set.
assessment.maturity: Correlated and superconducting states have been reproduced by many groups worldwide, but the microscopic origin of the superconductivity is still debated. The discovery is recent (2018) but the confirmation is broad.
uncertainties: Pairing mechanism is unresolved, so the physical interpretation is not yet stable.
Condensed-matter topic outside my expertise; I would lean on colleagues for the allocation of credit among theorists and experimenters.
Possible overlap with moire work by other groups not in the credited names.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Silicon microstrip and hybrid pixel detectors underpin vertex tracking in nearly every modern collider experiment, including the Higgs and heavy-flavour measurements, and spread to X-ray imaging at synchrotrons. As a detector builder I regard this as a foundational technology enabling many discoveries, but Nobel recognition for enabling instrumentation needs the prize criteria of an invention of 'greatest benefit' and the committee has been selective.
assessment.attribution: Heijne is the pioneer of silicon-detector concepts at CERN, Parker built the first microstrip detectors with Kemmer-type planar technology, and Campbell led the hybrid pixel chips (Medipix/Timepix). Kemmer, Hyams and Rancoita-era contributors are not on the list, and the micro-strip and pixel parts are two distinct inventions that might need different recognition.
assessment.maturity: Widely deployed for decades, completely proven and independent. The recognition is overdue rather than premature.
uncertainties: Compound candidate: strip and pixel detectors are different inventions with different inventors.
Whether the committee will treat enabling detector technology as a physics discovery or invention in the sense of Nobel's will.
Missing key contributors such as Josef Kemmer.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The EHT produced the first image of a black hole shadow in M87* and later Sgr A*, combining global VLBI at 1.3 mm with heavy calibration and imaging work. It is a striking measurement and a technical feat of an instrument network, and gives a direct test of strong-field gravity.
assessment.attribution: Falcke proposed the shadow imaging idea (with Melia and Agol) and Doeleman led the VLBI development and the collaboration. Zensus helped build the network. But the work is by a collaboration of more than 300 people, and the ideas of Bardeen and Luminet precede it, so a three-person prize would be hard to justify. I therefore propose two names.
assessment.maturity: Two sources imaged and the shadow size is consistent with GR, but constraints on alternative theories are still weak and polarimetric and time-resolved results are developing. Reasonably confirmed, though early.
uncertainties: Large-collaboration attribution problem and the earlier theoretical shadow work.
Limited independent confirmation, since only the EHT does this.
Image reconstruction depends on analysis assumptions.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: WMAP delivered precision full-sky CMB maps and fixed the parameters of the Lambda-CDM model to a few percent: age, geometry, baryon and dark-matter densities, and the reionisation epoch. It is a prime example of a space instrument whose calibration and systematics control produced a lasting result.
assessment.attribution: Bennett was the PI and led the mission, Page was a key instrument and design lead, and Spergel led the cosmological analysis and interpretation. The credit is reasonable, but the CMB has already been honoured in 2006 (Mather, Smoot) and 2019 (Peebles), and Planck later superseded WMAP, so the committee may see the marginal discovery as incremental.
assessment.maturity: Fully confirmed by Planck, ACT and SPT. Recognition would be late rather than premature, but the novelty is smaller than that of the first detection.
uncertainties: Whether precision refinement counts as a distinct discovery after the earlier CMB prizes.
Role of Planck and ground-based teams in the credit.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: BB84 and E91 established quantum key distribution as the first practical quantum-information protocol, with security grounded in quantum mechanics and a clear path to secure communication through fibre and satellite links. This connects directly to the sensing and cryptography applications that recent prizes have highlighted.
assessment.attribution: Bennett and Brassard authored BB84, and Ekert authored the entanglement-based E91 protocol, which connects to Bell tests (2022 prize). The three names form a natural configuration, though Wiesner's earlier conjugate-coding idea and Bennett's other work create a minor allocation question.
assessment.maturity: Demonstrated in commercial systems and satellite links (e.g. Micius), and the protocols are well proven in principle, although practical security with device imperfections remains an active topic.
uncertainties: Quantum information is outside my expertise and I would rely on colleagues on whether this is physics versus information theory.
Wiesner's earlier unpublished idea and its relation to BB84.
Overlap with the 2022 prize on entanglement and Bell tests.
